Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah's blessings and peace be upon our Prophet Muhammad, and upon his family and companions, and those who follow them in goodness until the Day of Judgment.

We begin this session with what Allah has facilitated of the tafsir of Surah al-'Adiyat.

Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿By the racers, panting, (1) And the producers of sparks, striking (2) And the chargers at dawn, (3) Raising thereby dust (4) And cleaving thereby into the center [of the enemy] en masse﴾ [al-'Adiyat 1–5] to the end of the surah.

It is not hidden from anyone that this is an oath: ﴿By the racers﴾, and that ﴿al-'Adiyat﴾ is an adjective of a omitted noun. So what is this omitted noun? Is the intended meaning the horses, i.e., "and by the horses that race," or the camels, i.e., "and by the camels that race"?

On this there are two opinions among the exegetes. Some of them said: the omitted noun is the camels, and the estimated phrase is "and by the camels that race," meaning the camels that run from 'Arafat to Muzdalifah and then to Mina, during the rites of Hajj. They argued for this by saying that this surah is Meccan, and that there was no jihad with horses in Makkah for which they would be sworn by.

As for the second opinion, held by the majority of exegetes—and it is the correct one—the omitted noun is the horses, and the estimated phrase is "and by the horses that race." The racing horses were known to the Arabs even before jihad was legislated; there were horses that charged against their enemies, rightly and wrongly, before Islam. As for after Islam, horses charge against their enemies only rightfully.

Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿al-'Adiyat﴾, and al-'Adi is the active participle from al-'Adw, which is quick walking and dashing.

As for His words ﴿dabhan﴾, ad-Dabh is what is heard from the bellies of horses when they run swiftly, producing a sound that comes out of their chests, and this indicates the strength and intensity of their running.

﴿Fa'l-Muriyati qadhan﴾: ﴿al-Muriyat﴾ is from (awra), meaning "struck (qadaha)," and it refers to striking fire, when stones strike one another, as is well known to us in the flint stone (hajar al-Marw); when you strike one part of it against another, it produces sparks.

These [camels] [sic—context refers to the horses], due to the strength and intensity of their running and the striking of the ground with their hooves, when they strike the stone they strike the second stone; it strikes the second stone and then sparks fire; this is due to their strength, the strength of their running, and their striking of the ground, ﴿fa'l-Muriyati qadhan﴾.

﴿Fa'l-Mughirati subhan﴾, i.e., those that raid at dawn upon the enemy, and this is the best time to raid the enemy... ﴿al-Mughirat subhan﴾, i.e., those that raid their enemy in the morning, and this is the best kind of raid upon the enemy, to be at dawn, because they are in heedlessness and sleep, and even if they wake from the raid they will be lethargic and exhausted. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, chose for the oath by these horses the best time for raiding, which is dawn. "The Prophet ﷺ would not raid a people at night, but would wait; if it became morning and he heard an adhan, he would refrain, and otherwise he would raid." [Narrated by al-Bukhari (610) from Anas ibn Malik that the Prophet ﷺ, when he raided a people with us, would not raid until morning and look; if he heard an adhan he would refrain from them, and if he did not hear an adhan he would raid them. He said: We set out toward Khaybar, and we reached them at night. When it was morning and he did not hear an adhan, he mounted, and I mounted behind Abu Talhah, and my foot touched the foot of the Prophet ﷺ. He said: They came out to us with their baskets and their shovels, and when they saw the Prophet ﷺ they said: "Muhammad, by Allah, Muhammad and the army!" When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw them he said: "Allah is greater, Allah is greater, Khaybar is ruined; indeed when we descend upon the courtyard of a people, evil is the morning of those who were warned."]

﴿Fa'atharna bihi naq'an﴾, i.e., they raised by this running and this raid ﴿naq'an﴾, which is the dust that rises from the intensity of the running; when horses run hard upon the ground, dust arises from their charging and retreating.

﴿Fa-wasatna bihi jam'an﴾, i.e., they penetrated through this dust into ﴿jam'an﴾, i.e., masses of enemies; that is, they have no limit, and their goal is only reached in the midst of the enemies. This is the utmost of the benefits of horses, although all horses are good, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Good is tied to the forelocks of horses until the Day of Resurrection." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2850) and Muslim (1873/98), from the hadith of 'Urwah ibn al-Ja'd al-Bariqi, may Allah be pleased with him.]

Allah, the Exalted, swore by these racers—these horses that have reached the utmost goal, which is raiding the enemy and penetrating the midst of the enemy without fear, fatigue, or boredom.

Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah's blessings and peace be upon our Prophet Muhammad, and upon his family and companions, and those who follow them in goodness until the Day of Judgment.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 100, verse 6:

As for the matter sworn to (al-muqsam 'alayh), it is man (al-insan). Allah says: ﴿Indeed, man is to his Lord ungrateful﴾ [al-'Adiyat 6]. The word "man" (al-insan) here refers to the species (al-jins); that is, if the human species is not granted guidance, it is ungrateful for the blessings of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says: ﴿And man carried it. Indeed, he was a wrongdoer, ignorant﴾ [al-Ahzab 72]. It has also been said that "man" here refers to the disbeliever, in which case the general term is used to mean the specific. The more apparent view is that it is meant in its general sense, and that the human species, were it not for Allah's guidance, would be ungrateful to its Lord, Mighty and Majestic.

Al-kanud (ungrateful) is al-kafur (the one who denies blessings); that is, one who disbelieves in the blessings of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Allah provides for him, and by this provision he increases in arrogance and aversion. Indeed, among people is one who transgresses when he sees himself independent of Allah, and how much wealth has corrupted the children of Adam! So he is ungrateful for the blessings of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, denying the blessings of Allah, not fulfilling their thanks, and not performing obedience to Allah, because he is ungrateful for the blessings of Allah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 100, verse 7:

﴿And indeed he is, to that, a witness.﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 7] ﴿Indeed, he﴾: the pronoun is said to refer to Allah; that is, Allah, the Exalted, bears witness against the servant that he is ungrateful for the blessing of Allah. It is also said that it refers to the human being himself; that is, the human being bears witness against himself to his disbelief in the blessing of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The correct view is that the verse encompasses both meanings: Allah is a witness over what is in the heart of the son of Adam and over his deeds, and the human being is also a witness against himself. However, he may acknowledge this testimony in this world, or he may not acknowledge it, and so he bears witness against himself on the Day of Resurrection, as Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands and their feet will testify against them as to what they used to do﴾ [an-Nur: 24].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 100, verse 8:

﴿Wa-innahu﴾ i.e., man, ﴿li-hubbi al-khayr la-shadid﴾ [al-'Adiyat 8]. "Al-khayr" (the good) here is wealth, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿It is prescribed for you that when death approaches one of you, if he leaves behind wealth, [he should make] a bequest﴾ [al-Baqarah 180], i.e., if he leaves behind much wealth. So "al-khayr" is wealth, and man's love of wealth is an evident matter. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And you love wealth with immense love﴾ [al-Fajr 20]. You hardly find anyone who is free from intense love of wealth. As for love in general, this is established for every person: there is no person who does not love wealth. But the intensity differs; not everyone has the same intensity. Some people love the amount of wealth that suffices them and makes them independent of the servants of Allah, some people want more, and some people want more and more. The main point is that every person is a lover of "al-khayr," i.e., of wealth, but people differ from one person to another in the degree of intensity.

Then, Allah the Exalted reminded man of a state he cannot avoid, saying: ﴿Does he not know that when what is in the graves is scattered forth [al-'Adiyat 9]﴾, so that he would act accordingly and not make wealth his concern.

﴿Does he not know﴾, i.e., does he not become certain, ﴿when what is in the graves is scattered forth﴾, i.e., spread out and brought to light. For people will come out of their graves to the Lord of the worlds as if they were scattered locusts, all coming out with a single cry; ﴿It will be but a single shout, and at once they will all be brought before Us [Ya-Sin 53]﴾.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And what is in the breasts is made known﴾ [al-'Adiyat 10]. That is: what is in the hearts of intentions and deeds of the heart, such as reliance upon Allah (tawakkul), desire (raghbah), fear of Allah (rahbah), dread (khawf), hope (raja'), and whatever is similar to these.

Here, Allah the Mighty and Majestic made the main matter (al-'umdah) what is in the breasts, as He said: ﴿On the Day when the secrets are tested. Then he will have no power nor any helper﴾ [at-Tariq 9-10]. This is because in this world people are treated according to what is apparent. Even the hypocrite is treated as a Muslim is treated in reality. But in the Hereafter, the reckoning is according to what is in the heart. For this reason it is obligatory upon us to attend to our hearts before everything else, before the (outward) deeds, because the heart is the axis on which everything turns, and it is upon it that the recompense will be on the Day of Resurrection. For this reason He said: ﴿What is in the breasts is made known﴾.

The connection between the two verses is that the scattering of what is in the graves is the bringing forth of the bodies from the depths of the earth, and the making known of what is in the breasts is the bringing forth of what the breasts conceal. So the scattering of what is in the graves is about what the earth conceals, and here it is about what the chest conceals. The harmony between them is clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 100, verse 11:

﴿Indeed, their Lord is, concerning them that Day, certainly Acquainted.﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 11] Meaning: indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is Acquainted with them, that is, with the servants. He said ﴿bihim﴾ (with them, in the plural) and did not say "bihi" (with him, in the singular), even though "al-insan" (the human being) is singular in wording; but in meaning it is plural. That is, He returned the pronoun to "al-insan" according to its meaning, because the meaning of ﴿Indeed, al-insan﴾ is "indeed every human being." He tied the knowledge to that Day, ﴿Indeed, their Lord is, concerning them that Day, certainly Acquainted﴾, because it is the Day of Recompense and Reckoning. Otherwise, Allah, exalted is He, is All-Knowing and All-Aware on that Day and before it. He, Majestic and Exalted, knows what has been, what will be, and what would have been had it not been, how it would have been.

This is the brief explanation of this great surah, and whoever wishes for an extended treatment should refer to the books of tafsir that expand on this matter. We are only pointing to the meanings in a concise manner. At the beginning of this blessed section we explained that we chose this surah because people often hear it in the audibly recited prayers of Maghrib, 'Isha' and Fajr.

We ask Allah for guidance and success for us and for you, and that He make us among those who recite the Book of Allah with its due recitation. Indeed, He is capable of all things.
